howDoI.q: How do I paint a beam of light over a wall?
How do I let the wall show through a beam?
How do I make a beam fade at its edges?
How do I make fog that hides far hills a little more than near ones?
How do I make fog that drifts?
How do I give a moving light a glow?

pages.head: Welcome
pages.html:
Welcome

Beams and Fog is a Starter: a small game that shows a few Game-Maker ideas, with signs in the levels that say what you are looking at. This one is about light and fog. A game has no see-through colors, so a beam of light, a haze or a glow is painted in dots: one pixel in two, or one in four, so what is behind the dots shows through the gaps. The eye mixes the two. It has three short levels and takes a few minutes.

Play it first. Then open it in Game-Maker (Edit a copy on the home page keeps the original safe) and read the pages here, the How this level is made page of each level in particular. Related Starters: Little Shadows dithers shadows under things, Lights Out paints rings of shade into blocks, and Don't Get Seen has searchlights that are solid.

pages.head: Level 1: The Beams
pages.html:
Level 1: The Beams

A dark brick hall with three lamps hung from the ceiling. Each lamp shines a beam down onto the floor. The first beam is solid: one flat pale color, and the bricks under it are gone. The second is a checkerboard: one pixel in two is light, so the bricks stay. The third has three densities: thick in the middle, thinner toward the edge, thinnest at the very edge, so it fades.

Walk into each beam. Lian stands in front of all three, so they are easy to see in every one. The door at the end leads on to the fog.

pages.head: How this level is made
pages.html:
How the beams are made

  • A background block has no clear pixels. Every pixel of a wall block replaces what was behind it, so a beam over the wall cannot be a see-through picture on top. Instead the beam is made of twins of the wall block: wallLit25, wallLit50, wallLit75 and wallLit100. Each is the same bricks with the light's color painted on some of the pixels. The map simply uses a twin wherever the beam falls.
  • Density is how many pixels are painted. 50 is a checkerboard, 25 is one pixel in a 2 by 2 square, 75 is three of four, and 100 is every pixel, which is the solid beam. The dots in the pictures below are in purple.
  • The floor has twins too (floorLit25 to floorLit100), where the beam lands.
  • The beam is a cone. It opens from the bulb to the floor, and its edges run at an angle. Blocks the beam covers all over are the plain twins: the first lamp uses wallLit100, the second wallLit50, the third 75 in the middle, then 50, then 25 toward the edge. A block an edge cuts through gets a twin of its own (beam0, beam1 and so on) with the light painted only where the beam falls.
  • The patterns join. A block is 20 pixels wide and tall, an even number, so a pattern that starts at a block's corner carries on in the next block with no seam. If you draw your own, start every block's pattern at its own top-left pixel.

pages.head: Level 2: The Fog
pages.html:
Level 2: The Fog

A valley with three layers of hills, far to near. The left half has solid fog: each layer is covered in one flat pale color, the farthest the palest. It looks like fog, but the little trees on the hills are gone. The right half has dithered fog: dots of the same pale color, thick on the far hills (75 percent), thinner on the middle ones (50) and thin on the near ones (25). The trees show through. Two banks of fog drift across this half, a slow far one and a faster near one.

Walk across, then stand under the drifting fog. The door leads to the glow.

pages.head: How this level is made
pages.html:
How the fog is made

  • Fog is a color over distance. Far things look paler. Each layer of hills is two rows of blocks, a ridge row and a fill row, and each has its own set of pictures: hill.solid.0.ridge0 is the farthest layer in the solid half, hill.dither.2.fill1 the nearest in the dithered one. The hills are drawn first with their trees, then the fog is painted over the hill pixels only, never the sky.
  • Solid or dots. In the solid half every hill pixel is changed to that layer's pale color. In the dithered half only the painted pixels are, at 75, 50 or 25 percent, so a dark pixel in every few is a tree or a hill showing through. The farther the hill, the thicker the fog.
  • The ridge repeats every three blocks. The hill's edge is drawn as a wave that is 60 pixels long, so three ridge pictures (ridge0, ridge1, ridge2) join end to end in any order of three, and the hills run on for as long as the level does with no more blocks.
  • Drifting fog is a monster. A monster's picture can have clear pixels (color 255), so fog that moves is a monster whose picture is a puff painted in dots, thick in the middle and thin at the edge. Three puffs side by side, all the same monster with the same path, make a bank that stays together. The far bank has speed 1 and the near one speed 2, so the near fog crosses faster, as near things seem to.
  • No flicker. The fog moves across the screen but its pictures never change, so nothing flashes. A picture that did change should do so no more than about three times a second.

pages.head: Level 3: The Glow
pages.html:
Level 3: The Glow

The hall again, with three lanterns floating to and fro along the wall. The first has a solid halo, a pale disc that hides the bricks under it. The second has a checkerboard halo: the bricks show through. The third has halos in rings, thick in the middle and thinner outward, so the glow fades.

Jump up into a lantern. Lian stays easy to see in front of each. The last door ends the game.

pages.head: How this level is made
pages.html:
How the glow is made

  • A light that moves is a monster. A monster's picture can have clear pixels, so the wall shows through them with no twins of the wall needed. Each lantern is a group of nine monsters, three by three: a little lantern in the middle one and a halo painted around it in dots across all nine. The halo's pixels outside its circle are all clear.
  • Solid, checkerboard, rings. lamp.solid (nine pieces, lamp.solid.00 to lamp.solid.22) paints every pixel of the halo's disc. lamp.dither paints every other pixel. lamp.soft paints the inner part at 75 percent, the middle at 50 and the outer ring at 25.
  • Nine blocks. A monster is one 20 by 20 block, so a big halo is several monsters with the same path and speed side by side, as the fog's puffs are in the fog level. Here each of the nine is its own monster (27 in all), because each holds a different piece of the 60 by 60 halo.
  • The path is the same for all three: right six blocks and back, speed 1, each in its own stretch of the hall.

pages.head: What it cannot do
pages.html:
What it cannot do

These are the engine's limits, so you can plan around them.

  • It cannot lighten what is under it. A picture's pixels replace what is under them or they are clear. There is no see-through color and no brightening, so a beam is a color painted in dots, the same pale yellow over a dark wall and a bright one.
  • A background block cannot be clear. That is why the beams and the fog are twins of the blocks they fall on, and why a beam over a new kind of wall needs a new set of twins.
  • A moving dither can shimmer. A monster's checkerboard moves with it and the wall does not, so the dots and the bricks can fight as it passes. Slow monsters and plain walls look best.
  • A monster is one block. A big moving glow or bank of fog is several monsters. They stay together only while they have the same path and speed and start together.
  • The fog does not change what Lian looks like. They are drawn in front, in their own colors. A character is drawn over a background block, so fog in front of Lian would need a monster over them.
  • Flashing. A picture that changes more than about three times a second can bother people. Nothing here changes pictures that quickly.

pages.head: Make it yours
pages.html:
Make it yours

Try one change at a time, and play after each:

  • In beams.bbl, redraw wallLit50 with a paler or a darker color and see what the checkerboard does.
  • Draw a wallLit75 with a different pattern (every third pixel clear) and see if it looks like a different light.
  • In fog.bbl, make the far hills' fog 25 and the near ones 75 and see how the valley seems to turn inside out.
  • Give a lantern a different speed in the Monsters tab, and then try a halo that is a single color but a different size.
  • Draw a ring of light for a torch on the wall: a lit twin of the brick, in a round patch, and a darker twin around it.
